Parallel planes have parallel normal vectors.

Example

The coefficients of are read straight off as the normal vector (from the scalar equation of a plane in the previous lecture). Here , so the normals are parallel and the planes are parallel. They are two different planes because the right-hand sides do not match in the same ratio: doubling the first equation gives , not .

Fact

The angle between two intersecting planes is the angle between their normals.

Explanation (added)

Tilt one plane relative to the other and its normal tilts by exactly the same amount, so the two angles are equal. This turns a question about planes into the “angle between two vectors” formula from 12.3.

0412.6 Cylinders

Definition

A cylinder is a surface (in ) consisting of all lines parallel to a given line passing thru a given plane curve.

The lines are called “rulings”.

Examples
Explanation (added)

In this course “cylinder” means much more than a tin can. The curve can be any plane curve (a circle, an ellipse, a parabola, a cubic), and the rulings only have to be parallel to each other — they do not have to be perpendicular to the curve’s plane. The practical test: if one of is missing from the equation, the surface is a cylinder whose rulings are parallel to the axis of the missing variable.

05Quadric surfaces

Definition

The graph of a deg-2 eqn in 3 variables is called a quadric surface:

– By rotating and translating, we can always write the eqn of a quadric surface in form:

Explanation (added)

This is the 3-D version of the conic equation above. Rotating the axes removes the mixed terms ; translating (completing the square, as with the sphere in 12.1) removes the first-degree terms where possible. What is left is either “all three variables squared” (form 1: ellipsoids, cones, hyperboloids) or “two squared and one to the first power” (form 2: paraboloids).

How to Draw It Like the Board

  1. Axes: up, right, coming toward you diagonally (lower-left). Tick each unit.
  2. Intercepts: mark , , with dots, read straight from the denominators .
  3. Three traces: connect the dots in each coordinate plane:
    • gives , the flat “equator.”
    • gives , the front-to-back loop.
    • gives , the side-to-side loop.
  4. Dashes: draw the back halves (the side) dashed.
  5. Outline: wrap one smooth curve around everything.
Explanation (added)

A trace is the curve you get by slicing the surface with a plane parallel to a coordinate plane — set one variable equal to a constant . For the right-hand side must be positive for there to be a curve, so the surface only exists for (single points at ); likewise and . All three families of traces are ellipses, so the surface is an ellipsoid: a stretched sphere with semi-axes , and .

06The six quadric surfaces

A summary of Stewart’s Table 1 (the original table from the PDF is in the right column) together with the typed “how to spot each one” chart.

Ellipsoid

Every trace is an ellipse. When it is a sphere.

Spot it by: All squared, all ,

Cone

Horizontal traces: ellipses. Vertical traces , : hyperbolas when , a pair of lines when .

Spot it by: All squared, after moving terms, one sign different

Elliptic paraboloid

Horizontal traces: ellipses. Vertical traces: parabolas. The first-power variable gives the axis.

Spot it by: One variable not squared, other squares same sign

Hyperboloid of one sheet

Horizontal traces: ellipses. Vertical traces: hyperbolas. The axis is the variable with the negative coefficient.

Spot it by: All squared, , one minus

Hyperbolic paraboloid

Horizontal traces: hyperbolas. Vertical traces: parabolas. (Drawn here with , as in Stewart.)

Spot it by: One variable not squared, squares opposite signs

Hyperboloid of two sheets

Horizontal traces : ellipses when or . Vertical traces: hyperbolas. Two minus signs, two sheets.

Spot it by: All squared, , two minuses

SurfaceStandard formSpot it by
Cylindere.g. One variable missing
Explanation (added)

A fast way to classify: count the squared variables and the minus signs. Three squares: no minus → ellipsoid; one minus → hyperboloid of one sheet (or a cone if the constant is ); two minuses → hyperboloid of two sheets. Two squares and one first-power variable: same signs → elliptic paraboloid; opposite signs → hyperbolic paraboloid. A variable missing altogether: cylinder.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • “Find the angle between the planes … and find parametric (or symmetric) equations of their line of intersection.”
  • “Find the distance from the point … to the plane …”, or “find the distance between the parallel planes …”.
  • “Describe and sketch the surface” for an equation with a missing variable (a cylinder), e.g. or .
  • “Use traces to sketch and identify the surface”, e.g. or — find the traces , , , name each family of curves, then name the surface.
  • “Reduce the equation to one of the standard forms, classify the surface” (complete the square first), or match equations to pictures.
